Nate Koppikar wasn’t much older than me: We both came of age after the financial crisis. He often used the word consequences to describe this period, like he was contemplating a scale of justice that existed only in his head. After 2008, the scales had tipped too far. “People on the bottom end of the spectrum faced extreme consequences, where they were thrown out of their homes that they should not have bought,” he said. “And on the high end, they also made terrible decisions, but they were given get-out-of-jail-free cards, and they have gotten phenomenally richer.” When Koppikar told this story, or any of the others involving the scales, an incredulous smile would break across his face, as if to say: This is absurd and we both know it.

After graduating from the Wharton School of Business and a stint on Wall Street, Koppikar found himself working at a long-short fund on the West Coast, where he was tasked with picking undervalued stocks and shorting overvalued shares. The Bay Area was home to a small community of short sellers who spent most of their time finding holes in the stories that Wall Street wanted everyone else to believe. This meant identifying a company whose share price was due a fall, then betting that this would happen. You’d borrow shares from a broker and sell them to someone else, with a promise to return the same number of shares in the same company to the original broker by a certain date. Once their price started to fall, you would buy back the shares you owed at the lower price, return them to the broker, and pocket the difference. They were, unsurprisingly, very unpopular with their targets, and often got accused of representing capitalism’s most sordid side. Viewed from another perspective, however, they were an example of markets working to correct pricing errors.

In 2019, Koppikar founded his own short fund, Orso—the Italian word for bear—with Scott Matagrano. Koppikar and Matagrano told me more than once that they identified with the underdog. This might have surprised the average underdog, given that they were paid handsomely for investing millions of dollars. Perhaps to resolve that dissonance, they had converged upon a sort of homegrown political theory, dividing the world into “bad guys” and everyone else. The bad guys were the ones who inflated share prices and deceived their investors. Yet as the number of investigative journalists had shrunk and white-collar prosecutions had reached record lows, rooting out bad guys had become a dying art. Short sellers therefore occupied a curious position: Pretty much the only people willing to make trouble and ask awkward questions about company valuations were self-interested anti-heroes like this.

Koppikar and Matagrano soon turned their attention to the realm of private equity, which they viewed as a cancer that had metastasized in the years after the financial crisis. Koppikar called it a “Ponzi scheme.” Matagrano was similarly caustic. “You know, I’m a dyed-in-the-wool conservative,” he told me. “But at the same time, I see how much the United States has devolved into this cronyist economy. And private equity really is one of the [biggest] examples of how your average person has seen the American dream get pulled further and further away from them.” For both of them, the sheer proliferation of private equity funds rang alarm bells. Since 2008, the number had nearly doubled in the United States alone. Koppikar and Matagrano weren’t alone in thinking that these were the morbid symptoms of a market where too many people were chasing too few opportunities.

Wall Street was a place where you were more likely to be rewarded for unfounded optimism than rational pessimism. Naturally, Koppikar and Matagrano planned to capitalize on that.

They were up against a formidable adversary, and an increasingly well-connected one.

“In life you have to have a dream,” Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman told analysts on a call within days of Donald Trump’s first inauguration. Schwarzman’s dream, apparently, was to open up private equity to ordinary Americans. That was . . . odd. Private equity had never taken money from ordinary people. That was pretty much the point of it. The crash of 1929 had shown that most people needed honest, publicly available information in order to invest their money prudently, and private funds weren’t willing to hand over this information. That was why the SEC prevented them from raising capital from the general public.

Growth had become more important, it seemed, than making companies work better and selling them at a profit.

In any case, they had never seemed short of cash. Schwarzman’s industry had focused exclusively on smart money, targeting billionaires, family offices, university endowments, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and the like. These were known as “sophisticated” investors, since they hired teams of professionals to advise them on what to do with their wealth, and had experience navigating risks on their own. This very sophistication was part of what gave private equity its allure. It was a private members’ club only open to the world’s richest people, managed by Wall Street’s elite, who made that money grow like nobody else could.

And now this exclusive club wanted to expand its membership to ordinary Americans. There were two reasons that opening the gates to normal people seemed like a bad idea. First, “retail” investors, as they were known, often had no idea what they were doing. Second, they sometimes needed their money back in a hurry. This combination of naivety and necessary liquidity made them uniquely ill-suited to private equity funds, whose managers locked up money for years at a time and were notoriously selective in how they presented their returns. “You have to foresee that there will be people who have no idea of what they’re investing in, and will put a large percentage of their 401(k) into something like private equity, if it’s offered to them,” said Paul Secunda, an attorney who specializes in employee benefits law. “The PE guys get rich, but it’s not clear that middle-class participants benefit at all.”

That criticism was sharpened by the fact that private equity made a lot of money for its fund managers and much less for everyone else. A 2011 report produced by the World Economic Forum observed that the industry had been organized so that “most of the rents from these skills go to the fund managers themselves, rather than to the [investors].” Some of the industry’s most powerful investors—the Saudi royal family, say—had enough clout that they could negotiate better terms, or even come on board as “co-investors,” which meant they didn’t have to pay the fees that made the fund managers rich. Ordinary people would never have this clout. Instead, the risk was that they would become the mark that the fund managers could swindle for fees.

The Trump administration didn’t appear to see any problem with this, and in June 2020, Labor Secretary Eugene Scalia published an advisory letter announcing that Americans would soon be allowed to invest in private equity via their 401(k) accounts. It was supported by Jay Clayton, then the chair of the SEC (Clayton joined the board of Apollo, one of the world’s largest private equity funds, a few months after leaving office). This new encounter between private equity and middle-class Americans would, Scalia explained, help Americans saving for retirement gain access to investments “that often provide strong returns.” It would “level the playing field for ordinary investors.” It would also quite possibly allow fund managers to use these retirement savings as a means by which to transfer even more wealth from middle-class Americans to themselves.

This was alarming, but Koppikar was more concerned by a different question. Why did one of the richest industries on Earth need more money? The early cheerleaders for leveraged buyouts imagined they were creating value by undertaking surgery on bloated conglomerates. But many private equity firms now looked increasingly like those old conglomerates. Specialized funds had morphed into huge asset managers that did a bit of just about everything. They charged a 2 percent fee on the value of the assets they managed, which meant there was an incentive to keep growing bigger and bigger. Growth had become more important, it seemed, than making companies work better and selling them at a profit.

And to grow bigger required a constant inflow of new capital. The industry had already tapped just about every large pool of money in the world. Now it seemed to be running out of fuel. Meanwhile, many funds were having difficulty selling their assets. Managers had developed new tricks to paper over this fact: Some had started buying assets from themselves, while others were taking out loans against their portfolios in order to release cash to their investors without having to sell the actual assets at a discount. These techniques only served to disguise the troubling reality that fund managers were sitting on a bunch of wildly over-valued stuff that nobody wanted to buy. “They were just flipping [stuff] back and forth between one another,” Koppikar recalled.

Taken together, these two developments made the industry look increasingly like, well, a pyramid scheme. The focus was less about actually selling the overpriced hand lotions or herbal supplements, more on finding new housewives to recruit. Economists call this dynamic “Ponzi finance”: A rise in asset prices buoys the confidence of investors, breathless media coverage reinforces their conviction, and money flows into a market. That money is needed to support both the rise in prices and the loans that were made on the premise that the market would keep growing. But all this debt and risk-taking is very unstable. It therefore seemed quite revealing that, given the ear of government, private equity’s visionary elite could formulate no greater ambition than to get into the savings accounts of middle-class America.

At that point, most people didn’t want to imagine that a decades-long boom might be coming to an end. Certainly, the public pension funds that had invested more than one of every ten of their dollars in private equity didn’t want to think about this. But to Koppikar, witnessing these scenes was like seeing all of his doubts coalesce into a single thesis. His letter to Orso’s investors in the autumn of 2022 singled out a company that he euphemistically called “Bad Mark Co.” “The parent for BMC trades as if it is one of the greatest businesses in the history of the markets,” he wrote. “Our view is variant. We think the stock will see a significant correction in the coming months.”

The company he had singled out for his next short was Blackstone.

Koppikar rarely talked about his shorts at dinner parties or weddings. Telling somebody you were shorting their stock was a little like telling them their child was ugly. And this was Blackstone, for crying out loud. It was only possible to short the company because it was one of a handful of private equity firms that had taken the decision, in the aughts, to float themselves on the stock market. Most investment funds loved the firm. It was the most successful company in the world of alternative assets. “To many investors, advisers and finance columnists, Blackstone has the legendary Midas touch,” wrote one consultant. Going after it, Koppikar said, would be like “shorting God.”

If it goes well, the short seller might wind up looking like a genius. If it goes badly, they might end up losing their money and their credibility.

When a company’s management team discovers a short, they will often set about finding the flaws in the short seller’s thesis. If they can produce a convincing enough counternarrative, the company’s share price might go up, attracting new investors, who will push it up again. It’s a painful life lesson that a short seller can be right about a stock but wrong about how the markets will then behave; as John Maynard Keynes is once (perhaps apocryphally) supposed to have said: “Markets can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent.” A short seller may end up pushing the stock price upwards despite all of the evidence marshalled against it, and can end up suffering huge losses: There is no limit on how high a stock price can climb. This makes shorting a duel of public arguments in which the short seller is always the most exposed. If it goes well, they might wind up looking like a genius. If it goes badly, they might end up losing their money and their credibility.

Koppikar and Matagrano knew two things: They knew that Blackstone wanted to go after retail investors, and they knew that this strategy was flawed, because retail investors didn’t behave the same way as their usual customers. The question of how these two flaws would play out in practice was more difficult to answer.

In the weeks after his letter, Koppikar received a call from a contact who worked in the allocations business. “He said, ‘Listen, I got a bunch of clients that are in this BREIT. You’ve got to take a harder look at it.’” Blackstone Real Estate Investment Trust (BREIT) was a company that packaged real estate into bite-sized chunks, which Blackstone had created in 2017. Almost nobody in finance thought private REITs were a good idea (“about as appealing as a condemned apartment house beside a railroad track,” as one Forbes contributor had described them back in 2016). Shares in private REITs weren’t publicly traded, and were typically more expensive than their public equivalents, their price determined by insiders who were prone to inflating the value of properties. BREIT charged its investors an annual 1.25 percent fee on assets under management, and a 12.5 percent incentive fee if its returns exceeded 5 percent. By contrast, you could buy shares in a public REIT that would give you a broad sample of real estate, and you could sell those shares any time you wanted, all while paying a lower fee.

Even so, Blackstone seemed to think that it had something more special to offer, and by 2022, BREIT was one of the firm’s biggest success stories, at least on paper. According to Goldman Sachs, it accounted for about a fifth of the company’s annual fee revenues. It had swallowed up apartments, suburban houses, student dorms, data centers, and shopping malls. It bought the Bellagio in Las Vegas, and a seventy-six-story skyscraper designed by Frank Gehry. It bought a Florida complex for interns working at Walt Disney World. And all you needed to put money into BREIT was a net worth of at least $250,000, or a gross annual income of at least $70,000 and a net worth of at least the same. All you needed, in other words, was a decent job, a savings account, or a modest inheritance. To be clear, this wasn’t private equity, and had nothing to do with leveraged buyouts. Yet BREIT seemed like a trial run for a much bigger goal: to open the gates of giant firms like Blackstone to the middle classes.

The marrow of Koppikar and Matagrano’s thesis was this: Blackstone had created a shiny new product for people who should never have been investing with Blackstone. Now, the company was sitting on billions of dollars of their money, and at some point, it was going to get burned. Retail investors behaved more like mice than giants, scuttling between investments and playing the markets like a game. For most of them, investing was a hobby, not a full-time profession. And they sometimes needed their money back, to pay down the mortgage or cover their kid’s school fees. What would happen if they suddenly wanted to take it out of BREIT? Leafing through the prospectus for Blackstone’s mass-market product, Koppikar noticed a detail buried in its small print. BREIT only allowed its clients to redeem a certain percentage of their total assets each month. If withdrawals breached a monthly limit, and people began clamoring to take too much money out of the product, Blackstone could bring the shutters down and “gate” the trust. This wasn’t unusual: When pension funds invest in private equity, they expect to tie up their money for a number of years. But Blackstone was now dealing with a bunch of people who were used to withdrawing their money as easily as if they were at their bank.

It was during the summer of 2022 that Orso began to build up its position in Blackstone’s stock. By then, the real-estate market had slowed and people were warning of “zombie” tower blocks that were left empty after the pandemic. In San Francisco, as the pandemic receded, nearly a quarter of offices were vacant, and people openly wondered, now that the nation was working from home, whether commercial real estate had a future.

Yet Blackstone seemed impervious to these trends. On an investor call, Schwarzman suggested that was because rents for real estate across the United States had risen two to three times faster than inflation. Since most of the leases in Blackstone’s real estate portfolio were “shorter duration,” the firm could “reprice” these easily. “It’s because we own all this wonderful stuff in the right places,” he told an audience at Davos in early 2023. But this didn’t stand to reason. How could one company be insulated from the downturn in the rest of the market? Finally, in November that year, a news story confirmed what Koppikar and Matagrano had predicted. Bloomberg reported that investors in BREIT were taking their money out. The narrative was contagious: as soon as one group decided to pull their money, others would follow, and the effect would be similar to a bank run.

At a hotel in New York that December, Schwarzman took to the stage to address a conference organized by Goldman Sachs. He told the audience that recent concerns about BREIT were “baffling.” His firm had already announced that it would be limiting the money investors could withdraw, and was being hammered by redemptions. That week, Blackstone’s stock dropped by nearly 10 percent. The whole episode was already being described in the press as a cautionary tale about the perils of opening private equity to the public.

Meanwhile, Koppikar’s Wall Street peers had started to take a new interest in his ideas. The emails he was getting tended to follow one of two formats: Either people would urge him to recant, or they would say that they had been harboring similar suspicions. Institutional Investor, a prominent magazine in the private capital industry, ran a profile that presented Koppikar as an audacious gadfly who had dared to bite a racehorse. In 2022, the piece noted, Blackstone’s shares fell by more than 40 percent, more than double the decline of the S&P 500.

Koppikar and Matagrano couldn’t celebrate yet, though. Blackstone still had another card to play.

On a crisp January morning in 2024, a group of suited trustees took their seats inside a wood-paneled office in Oakland. Jagdeep Singh Bachher sat at the head of the table, wearing a silk pocket square in the same sky-blue shade as his turban. Bachher, the chief investment officer for the University of California’s pension fund, was responsible for $23.4 billion of workers’ retirement money. He spoke in a voice so smooth it almost smothered disagreement. On December 8, seven days after Blackstone prevented investors from taking their money out of BREIT, Bachher got on a call with Nadeem Meghji, the head of Blackstone’s American real estate division. “If we can be helpful,” Bachher said, “we’re here.” The call turned into a conversation that turned into an offer. Bachher pledged to invest $4 billion of workers’ savings into the floundering product. At the office in Oakland that afternoon, a hearing had been scheduled to discuss what seemed like a colossal bailout.

The atmosphere in the room was less like an investment meeting than a courtroom show on daytime TV. A group of campaigners had gathered in the visitors’ chamber. They wore yellow T-shirts printed with the logo of a plucky NGO that had spent the last six years trying to block Blackstone’s purchase of homes across California. One by one, each campaigner took a spot on the microphone to address Bachher and the board of trustees. Their speeches became angrier as the hour wore on. “Blackstone: You are a monster. Really, you are a monster,” said one campaigner. “You treat people like they’re trash,” said another, a diminutive woman whose frail appearance bore no relation to the vigor of her accusations.

To the campaigners, Bachher’s decision was close to sacrilege. He had taken the money saved by thousands of university workers, teaching staff and janitors, and invested it in a company that they regarded as one of the main causes of their hardship. California had one of the highest rates of homelessness across America, and rising rents in the state’s major cities meant 95 percent of the university’s service workers couldn’t afford a one-bed apartment near campus. “Through this partnership . . . the university is literally investing [workers’] hard-earned dollars in their own housing insecurity,” declared one union representative at the meeting.

Bachher had invited two of Blackstone’s most senior executives to speak. After the campaigners had settled down, they took to the floor. “We’re so pleased to be here, to create an opportunity for all of us to get to know one another better . . . and also to have an opportunity to clear up some of the misinformation,” said Kathleen McCarthy, the firm’s global head of real estate, addressing the investment committee. “And . . . one thing I reflect on . . . is just how I think we are such natural partners. Because similar to you, we focus intently on how we can generate high-quality results for the people and the institutions that depend on us, but do that in a way that is highly responsible and high integrity.”

It was a variation on a familiar argument, often repeated by lobbyists: The industry served hardworking teachers and firefighters by providing them with long-term retirement security. Whenever this argument was made, it tended to overlook a less palatable reality. While pension funds accounted for the majority of private equity dollars, they weren’t necessarily the most powerful or important investors, measured by the size of their individual investments. Sovereign wealth funds and family offices often had the power to extract better terms, since their single investments could be far larger. Admittedly, being the natural partner to billionaires and oil sheikhs had less of a comradely ring to it.

The stability of the institution depended less on whether it was doing a good job than on whether it had manufactured enough consent.

“It’s hard to escape the feeling that something has gone horribly wrong when giant sums of money are made by the asset management billionaires at the top of the heap, while the union members of the pension plans they are managing, and profiting from, can’t afford homes,” wrote Imogen Rose-Smith, a journalist who previously worked alongside Bachher, as a fellow in the Office of the Chief Investment Officer at the University of California. “If your pension is secure but you can’t afford a place to live because Blackstone et al. have bought up all the housing stock, are your best financial interests being served?” As the search for returns intensified, funds that invested workers’ money had started playing what Rose-Smith called the “poverty trade”: buying up essential services and wringing value from them to the detriment of middle- and working-class communities, even though members of those communities probably had money wrapped up in these same investments. Meanwhile, a few of the richest people on the planet were creaming off enormous fees from their retirement savings. Workers were getting squeezed in more than one direction.

So why did Bachher go ahead and hand over $4 billion of their money? He declined to give me an interview, so I can only speculate about his personal motivations. Still, a look at the small print suggests an agreement that worked out pretty well for his employers. In return for a $4 billion investment over six years, Blackstone offered the University of California a backstop of $1 billion of its own shares in BREIT as collateral. If Blackstone didn’t achieve its return targets, those shares would go to the university.

There were facts, and then there was narrative. Private equity enjoyed the support of countless politicians in Washington, who had been won over by a vast and well-connected infantry of lobbyists. In the words of David Swensen, an early evangelist, it was “a superior form of capitalism.” With a narrative like this, the facts didn’t stand a chance.

Blackstone bounced back. By October 2024, its stock was trading at a five-year high. The firm’s share price would rally so long as investors kept on pouring money into private equity, and so long as the wider industry’s connections allowed fund managers to shape their own destiny. The second Trump administration was a further vote of confidence. In July 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was signing an executive order allowing private equity into 401(k) plans, giving the industry precisely what it wanted.

By now, shorting private equity was a little like shorting the government. The stability of the institution depended less on whether it was doing a good job than on whether it had manufactured enough consent. So long as its supporters remained happy, the industry, much like the government, could stay powerful far longer than individuals could stay solvent. Koppikar and Matagrano had predicted that people would want their money back, and although that prediction came true, it still had no bearing on reality. Financially, the short hadn’t been a disaster, but nor had it been one of their more profitable theses (they were still shorting Blackstone’s stock in 2025). “If I had to be intellectually honest about this, I’d say that no matter how bad the news is, for private equity, nothing ever matters,” Koppikar told me.

There were, however, warning signs that the industry’s investors were getting tetchy. Between 2022 and 2024, the number of private equity deals dropped by 35 percent, and funds were sitting on a pool of unsold assets that amounted to $3.2 trillion. In early 2024, the management consultancy firm Bain issued a report that assessed the situation using panic-stricken metaphors. “The threat to returns is real,” it declared. “The word for this market is stalled.” Another phrase it used was “gasping for air.” The language was reminiscent of the crisis communications that Koppikar had witnessed in the months before the crash. In May that year, a journalist at the Financial Times discovered that private equity funds had actually taken in $1.5 trillion more from their investors in the preceding six years than they had paid back to them in returns.

Even pension fund managers seemed to be having second thoughts. In early 2024, Bachher told his fellow trustees that unless interest rates came down, the University of California’s pension fund would look to lower its exposure to private markets, at least for a period. Other pension funds and endowments were asking for their money back from previous investments before they committed to allocating more capital. Still others had decided to start shedding their stakes in private equity funds altogether, perhaps concluding that it was better to cut their losses than continue to hope. In 2024, fundraising plunged by 23 percent on the previous year, and the industry’s assets dropped in value for the first time in decades. As Koppikar wrote in a letter to his investors in the summer of 2025, “While nothing ever matters for now, empires are also lost to complacency.”
